seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: A few lines to acknowledge receipt of your letter with reply from Dr Gould . For a change I have been ill again with my throat. I shall write you fully on that interesting point tomorrow. Mr Richards consents to publish Exiles on conditions which my agent calls “disastrous”. I suspect the MS forwarded to Mr Quinn has gone astray. I received the Little Review and read your amusing sketch of sir Rabindranath Tagore but did not yet receive
Poetry nor Mr Eliot’s verses . I am glad you are ebullient and writing. My lame pen goes its cheerless way. My wife thanks for the kind mention of her. The Zurich daily thunderstorm is approaching so – Kindest regards to Mrs Pound and yourself

postscript.p: P.S. Can you publish music in the Little Review ?

div.note: On the reverse of this postcard, below JJ’s return address, Pound made two rough sketches of geometric shapes somewhat resembling the transepts and truncated nave of a cathedral.

After much effort, Pound had tracked down George Milbry Gould (1848-1922), the noted American ophthalmologist. Writing to JJ on 27 June 1917, Pound reported Dr. Gould’s opinion that JJ “should have gone to some trustworthy ophthalmic surgeon and been treated perhaps operated upon.” Gould recommended “Sir Anderson Critchett, in London” (Pound/Joyce 120). For Gould’s biography, see JJ to Pound, 13 April 1917, notes.
On 7 July 1917, JJ wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver: “I have been laid up for the past week with fever and tonsillitis. I am better today” (LI 103).

JJ’s Dubliners contract gave his London publisher Grant Richards the first refusal of Exiles, which JJ said he otherwise would have offered to Harriet Shaw Weaver’s Egoist Press (LI 107). JJ’s London literary agent, J.B. Pinker, wrote him on 2 July 1917 that he had received a note in which Richards confirmed that he would publish Exiles. Pinker added, “However was it that you signed such a disastrous agreement!” (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915–1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 221). JJ replied to Pinker angrily on 8 July 1917 that he had entered into the Dubliners contract “after a struggle of 9 years for the publication of my book – written in 1905,” and after “cost … in litigation and trainfare and postal expenses [of] about 3000 francs” (LII 399). Exiles was published simultaneously by Grant Richards in London and B.W. Huebsch in New York in May 1918. Weaver’s Egoist Press published a second English edition of 1,000 copies in 1921.

By early July 1917, Quinn had received the manuscript of the first act of Exiles (LI 104). A cablegram from Quinn to Pound dated 15 August 1917 confirmed that he had received acts two and three (Pound/Joyce 123).

The Bengali poet Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 and a British knighthood in 1915, which he renounced after the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Pound and Yeats enthusiastically promoted his poetry during 1912-1913. Pound’s satirical character sketch, “Jodindranath Mawhwor’s Occupation,” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 4, no. 1 (May 1917): 12-18.

Pound’s “Three Cantos,” an early, tentative approach to his epic poem, appeared in Poetry, vol. 10, nos. 3-5 (June, July, August 1917): 113-21, 180-88, 248-54, but he preferred that JJ read the revised version that would appear later in 1917 in his volume Lustra, published in New York in a private edition and also by Alfred A. Knopf (Pound/Joyce 121, 122). T.S. Eliot’s Prufrock and Other Observations was published in June 1917 by the Egoist Press in an edition partially subsidized by Ezra and Dorothy Pound. JJ received his copy on 22 October 1917 (LIII 510).
Pound wrote JJ on 27 June 1917 that he had been “writing ebulliently for days & feel like a dry sponge” (Pound/Joyce 120).
Pound added at the end of his letter of 27 June 1917 to JJ: “Amitiés à madame” (Pound/Joyce 120).
JJ was morbidly afraid of thunderstorms.
Pound replied on 17 July 1917 that “the Little Review cant [sic] cope with music. At least not for a year or two” (Pound/Joyce 122). For JJ’s reason for asking, see JJ to Pound, 9 July 1917.
